transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess what finally pushed me to come in is I keep making these small mistakes that I really should be catching. It’s not big dramatic stuff, but it’s enough that it’s starting to bother me.

Like, I go to the senior center and there’ll be a sign-up sheet or a class sheet, and I’ll write the wrong time down even though it’s right there in front of me. Or I’ll be doing something with wood at home, measure a board, think I’ve got it, and then cut it just a hair short because I missed some small detail or skipped over the fine print, so to speak. And then I’m standing there thinking, “How did I do that? I just looked at it.”

It’s those little errors, over and over, that make me feel like I’m not paying close enough attention even when I’m trying to.
Have you had this kind of trouble with attention and small careless mistakes for most of your life, or is this something that started only more recently?

No, it’s not just recent. I mean, I notice it more now, maybe because I have more time to think about it, but when I look back it was there pretty early.

Even in elementary school, the teachers would write things like, you know, “He’s bright,” or “He understands the material,” but then right underneath that it’d be, “forgets his books,” “loses homework,” “needs reminders to stay on task.” That sort of thing. I remember staring out the window a lot, just drifting, and unless the teacher came by or someone kind of pulled me back to what I was supposed to be doing, I’d get off track.

So, yeah, it feels like it’s been part of me for a long time. It just shows up differently now than it did when I was a kid.
Do these attention slips cause problems in more than one part of your life?

Yes, it does. I mean, it’s not ruining my whole life or anything, but it shows up in a few places, and that’s what’s started to worry me a little.

At the senior center, for example, I used to help out more with the do-it-yourself type workshops — little woodworking or repair things, nothing fancy — and I’ve kind of stepped back from helping lead those. Not because I don’t enjoy them, I really do, but I started getting nervous that I’d mix up a measurement or overlook some step and then everyone else would be following my mistake. It’s embarrassing, and I don’t want to be the reason something goes sideways.

And at home, my wife has had to start double-checking plans with me more than she used to. If we’re planning a family visit or something at the center, she’ll look over the time or the date or what I wrote down, just to make sure I didn’t copy it wrong or forget some detail. She’s kind about it, but I don’t like needing that. It makes me feel like I can’t quite trust myself with things I should be able to handle.
Have you been having trouble with your memory lately?

Memory? I’m not really sure how to answer that. I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed some big memory problem, like I don’t recognize people or I’m getting lost or anything like that. It’s more… sometimes I’ll wonder whether I forgot something or whether I just didn’t really take it in properly in the first place.

Like if I put something down and then can’t find it, I’ll think, “Is that memory, or was I just not paying attention when I set it there?” So I guess I’m not sure. I haven’t noticed anything that feels dramatically different, but I do get frustrated because it can feel like my mind didn’t hold onto the thing the way it should have.
Have these attention problems been getting worse over the past few years?

I don’t know if I’d say it’s been steadily getting worse for years and years, exactly. It’s more that it’s become noticeably harder to work around since we moved into the condo — that was about a year and a month ago now.

Before that, I think I had ways of compensating without thinking about it too much. But with the move and getting settled into a new place, there were just more little details to keep track of, and that’s when I started noticing it interfering more. So it may not be brand-new, but it’s been more obvious and more of a problem over this past year or so.
Have you gotten lost in places that should be familiar to you?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve had the usual moments where I take a wrong turn in a big parking lot or come out of a store and have to think for a second which direction the car is, but I wouldn’t say I’m getting lost in familiar places.

Around home, or the senior center, or places I normally go, I still know where I am. I haven’t had that experience of being somewhere I should know and suddenly feeling like I don’t recognize it. If that’s what you mean, then no, I haven’t noticed that.
Have you been feeling down or depressed much of the time lately?

I don’t think I’d say down or depressed much of the time, no. I mean, I have moments where I get discouraged or irritated with myself, especially when I feel like I’m not keeping up with things the way I should, but I don’t know that I’d call that depression.

It’s more like frustration, if that makes sense. I’m not waking up every day thinking everything is hopeless or anything like that. So… no, not much of the time, at least not in the way I understand depression.
Do you often feel anxious or worried?

I wouldn’t say often, no. I mean, I worry about things like anybody does — if there’s something I forgot to take care of, or if I’m running behind, I’ll get kind of tense about it. But I don’t feel like I’m anxious all the time, or that worry is just sitting on me for no reason.

It’s more situational, I guess. If something comes up, I might stew over it a bit, but then once it’s handled I usually settle back down. So I wouldn’t describe myself as a constantly worried person.
When you were working, did these attention problems ever cause trouble on the job?

Well, when I was working, I don’t remember it being a major job-threatening kind of problem, if that’s what you mean. I got by. But yes, there were definitely little mix-ups, and I’d have to compensate for them.

Since I’m not working now, I notice it more with things I do at the center or with family plans. Like, I used to help more with leading those DIY workshop things, where you’re showing people how to put something together or keeping track of materials and steps. And after a couple of times where I got turned around on the order of things or mixed up what was supposed to happen next, I kind of stepped back from being one of the people leading it. Not completely hiding from it, but I don’t like being the reason everybody gets confused.

And at home, my wife has started double-checking plans with me more. If we’re supposed to visit family or I’m helping coordinate something at the center, she’ll go over the time or the details so I don’t accidentally throw things off. It’s embarrassing, because it’s not like I don’t care — I do care — but sometimes the details don’t stay lined up the way I think they will.
Compared with how you were in your younger adult years, do you feel your attention is clearly worse now?

Clearly worse now… I’m not sure I’d say that exactly. It feels more noticeable now in some ways, maybe because life is less structured and people are relying on me to keep track of things. But when I think back, this isn’t completely new.

Even when I was a kid in elementary school, my teachers would write things like I was bright, or I understood the work, but then I’d forget to bring the right books, or I’d lose homework, or I’d be staring out the window unless somebody pulled me back to what I was supposed to be doing. My mother used to get those comments, and it was always sort of, “He can do it if he just stays on task,” that kind of thing.

So I don’t know if my attention is clearly worse now, or if I just don’t have as many people keeping me pointed in the right direction. It’s been around a long time.
Have you had any trouble managing your finances, like paying bills or balancing the checkbook?

Not so much the checkbook specifically — my wife is more on top of that side of things — but I do run into trouble when there are several things to handle in the same day. Like if I’ve got a couple errands, and something at the center to get ready for, and then an appointment too, I have a hard time putting it all in the right order.

I’ll think, “Okay, I’ll just do this first,” and then halfway through I realize I should’ve done the other thing first, or I’m missing something I needed to bring. So I start one thing, stop, switch to another, and then by the end I’m rushing around trying to catch up. It’s not that I can’t do the tasks, exactly — it’s more arranging them so they make sense that trips me up.
Have you been having trouble finding the right words when you speak?

Hmm… finding the right words? I don’t think that’s been a big thing for me, no. I mean, everybody has those moments where a word is on the tip of your tongue and you sort of wave your hand around like, “You know, that thing,” but I haven’t really noticed it as a pattern or something people are pointing out to me.

Sometimes if I’m tired or trying to explain something with too many pieces to it, I might talk in circles a bit before I get to the point, but I wouldn’t say I’m losing words exactly. At least, not that I’ve been aware of.
Have you been diagnosed with any medical or neurologic condition that affected your thinking?

Not that I know of, no. I mean, I’ve had the usual things doctors ask about over the years, but I haven’t been told I had some medical or neurological condition that was affecting my thinking.

I guess if you mean something like a stroke or a head injury or something along those lines, no one’s ever said that to me. At least, nothing I’ve been diagnosed with that I’m aware of.
Do you often find your mind drifting when you’re reading or when someone is talking to you?

Yes, that does happen. I notice it more in places like the senior center, where there’s a lot going on around me. If I’m filling out a form or trying to put something together, and people at the next table start talking, my attention just sort of jumps over there before I even mean for it to.

Same thing if my phone lights up — even if I don’t actually pick it up, I’ll glance at it, and then when I look back down I’ve lost where I was. Then I have to reread the line or figure out what step I was on, and it’s a little frustrating because I was doing fine until something pulled me away. It’s not constant every second, but it happens enough that I notice it.
Do you often put off or avoid tasks that require a lot of sustained mental effort, like paperwork, reading instructions, or organizing plans?

I’m not sure I’d say I avoid them on purpose, exactly. I mean, paperwork and instructions aren’t my favorite things, but I don’t know if that’s unusual or just… nobody really enjoys sitting down with a stack of forms, you know?

Sometimes I’ll put something aside if it feels like it’s going to take a lot of concentration, especially if I’m not in the right mood for it, but I can’t say I’ve really tracked how often that happens. If it’s something important, I usually get to it eventually. It might take me a little while to settle in and actually start, but I don’t know that I’d call it a major problem.

Organizing plans, I guess it depends what kind of plans you mean. If it’s something simple, I’m okay. If it has a lot of steps or details, I may sort of stare at it for a bit before I decide what to do first. But I’m not sure if that’s what you’re asking.
Do you often start tasks and then leave them unfinished?

Yes, sometimes. It’s not like I start a project and abandon it forever, but I do get kind of scattered when there are several things going on.

Like if I’ve got a few errands to run, and I’m also trying to get ready for a workshop, and then there’s an appointment later that same day, I have a hard time putting it all in the right order. I’ll start gathering something for the workshop, then remember I need to make a stop somewhere, so I’ll switch to that, and then I realize I haven’t left enough time for the appointment. So I end up starting one thing, stopping halfway, going to another thing, and then rushing around at the end trying to finish whatever I left hanging.

It’s more that I don’t always line things up well in my head, if that makes sense. I do usually get the important things done, but the process can be messy.
Do you often lose or misplace things you need, like keys, glasses, papers, or tools?

Yes, I do, more than I’d like to admit. It’s not usually something huge, but it’s those everyday things I need right then — my keys, my reading glasses, a tape measure if I’m doing something around the house, or that little bag I keep with card-game supplies in it.

What gets me is sometimes I’ll swear I just had the thing in my hand. Like I’ll set my glasses down for just a minute, and then a few minutes later I’m walking around checking the table, the counter, my pockets, the chair beside me — and it turns out they’re somewhere obvious, but not where I thought. Same with keys. I don’t lose them for days or anything, but I spend more time than I should hunting around for them.

It’s a little irritating because it’s usually when I’m trying to get ready to leave or get started on something, and then I’m delayed because I have to stop and do this whole search routine.
Do you often have trouble finishing tasks after someone gives you instructions, even when you understand what to do?

I’m not sure I’d say that happens a lot, at least not in a clear-cut way. If someone gives me instructions and I understand them, I can usually do the thing, especially if it’s fairly straightforward.

Where it gets a little fuzzy is if the instructions have a lot of parts, or if there’s a delay between being told and actually doing it. Then I might need to think back through it, like, “Wait, what was the order again?” But I don’t know if that’s really trouble finishing so much as needing a minute to get myself lined up.

If someone says, “Do this, then this, then this,” I generally get what they mean. I don’t usually just stop because I didn’t follow through. I guess I haven’t noticed that as one of my bigger issues, if that makes sense.

doctor.question: Have you had any trouble managing your finances, like paying bills or balancing the checkbook?

target_item.name: Organization_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When I have a few errands, a workshop to get ready for, and an appointment on the same day, I have trouble putting them in order and end up starting one thing, stopping, then rushing around at the end.
target_item.reason: The question is about managing a multi-step responsibility like bills or a checkbook, which most directly relates to difficulty organizing tasks and activities.

patient.answer:
Not so much the checkbook specifically — my wife is more on top of that side of things — but I do run into trouble when there are several things to handle in the same day. Like if I’ve got a couple errands, and something at the center to get ready for, and then an appointment too, I have a hard time putting it all in the right order.

I’ll think, “Okay, I’ll just do this first,” and then halfway through I realize I should’ve done the other thing first, or I’m missing something I needed to bring. So I start one thing, stop, switch to another, and then by the end I’m rushing around trying to catch up. It’s not that I can’t do the tasks, exactly — it’s more arranging them so they make sense that trips me up.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a clear decline from the patient’s longstanding baseline in another cognitive domain, especially language/word-finding, to distinguish lifelong ADHD from mild neurocognitive disorder or nonspecific attention complaints.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble finding the right words when you speak?

target_item.reason: The question is about word-finding difficulty when speaking, which is not covered by the listed ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Hmm… finding the right words? I don’t think that’s been a big thing for me, no. I mean, everybody has those moments where a word is on the tip of your tongue and you sort of wave your hand around like, “You know, that thing,” but I haven’t really noticed it as a pattern or something people are pointing out to me.

Sometimes if I’m tired or trying to explain something with too many pieces to it, I might talk in circles a bit before I get to the point, but I wouldn’t say I’m losing words exactly. At least, not that I’ve been aware of.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the attention problems are linked to a medical or neurologic condition rather than lifelong ADHD or nonspecific attention difficulty.

target_item.reason: The question asks about diagnosed medical or neurologic conditions affecting thinking, which is not covered by the provided ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Not that I know of, no. I mean, I’ve had the usual things doctors ask about over the years, but I haven’t been told I had some medical or neurological condition that was affecting my thinking.

I guess if you mean something like a stroke or a head injury or something along those lines, no one’s ever said that to me. At least, nothing I’ve been diagnosed with that I’m aware of.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has classic inattentive ADHD symptoms beyond careless mistakes, especially difficulty sustaining attention during reading or conversations, to distinguish lifelong ADHD from a nonspecific concentration complaint.
doctor.question: Do you often find your mind drifting when you’re reading or when someone is talking to you?

target_item.name: Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: At the senior center, if people are talking at the next table or my phone lights up, my mind jumps over there and I lose my place in what I was filling out or building.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about the mind drifting away from reading or conversation, which most directly matches distractibility and losing focus due to other stimuli or thoughts.

patient.answer:
Yes, that does happen. I notice it more in places like the senior center, where there’s a lot going on around me. If I’m filling out a form or trying to put something together, and people at the next table start talking, my attention just sort of jumps over there before I even mean for it to.

Same thing if my phone lights up — even if I don’t actually pick it up, I’ll glance at it, and then when I look back down I’ve lost where I was. Then I have to reread the line or figure out what step I was on, and it’s a little frustrating because I was doing fine until something pulled me away. It’s not constant every second, but it happens enough that I notice it.

doctor.intent: Differentiate ADHD, predominantly inattentive type from nonspecific attention/concentration difficulties by checking for another core inattentive symptom beyond distractibility and careless mistakes.
doctor.question: Do you often put off or avoid tasks that require a lot of sustained mental effort, like paperwork, reading instructions, or organizing plans?

target_item.reason: The question is most directly about avoiding or putting off tasks requiring sustained mental effort, which is not covered by the listed symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d say I avoid them on purpose, exactly. I mean, paperwork and instructions aren’t my favorite things, but I don’t know if that’s unusual or just… nobody really enjoys sitting down with a stack of forms, you know?

Sometimes I’ll put something aside if it feels like it’s going to take a lot of concentration, especially if I’m not in the right mood for it, but I can’t say I’ve really tracked how often that happens. If it’s something important, I usually get to it eventually. It might take me a little while to settle in and actually start, but I don’t know that I’d call it a major problem.

Organizing plans, I guess it depends what kind of plans you mean. If it’s something simple, I’m okay. If it has a lot of steps or details, I may sort of stare at it for a bit before I decide what to do first. But I’m not sure if that’s what you’re asking.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has a persistent pattern of poor task completion/disorganization that supports ADHD rather than a nonspecific concentration complaint.
doctor.question: Do you often start tasks and then leave them unfinished?

target_item.name: Organization_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When I have a few errands, a workshop to get ready for, and an appointment on the same day, I have trouble putting them in order and end up starting one thing, stopping, then rushing around at the end.
target_item.reason: The question is about starting tasks and not completing them, which in this profile is best reflected by difficulty organizing multiple tasks and ending up starting one thing, stopping, and rushing later.

patient.answer:
Yes, sometimes. It’s not like I start a project and abandon it forever, but I do get kind of scattered when there are several things going on.

Like if I’ve got a few errands to run, and I’m also trying to get ready for a workshop, and then there’s an appointment later that same day, I have a hard time putting it all in the right order. I’ll start gathering something for the workshop, then remember I need to make a stop somewhere, so I’ll switch to that, and then I realize I haven’t left enough time for the appointment. So I end up starting one thing, stopping halfway, going to another thing, and then rushing around at the end trying to finish whatever I left hanging.

It’s more that I don’t always line things up well in my head, if that makes sense. I do usually get the important things done, but the process can be messy.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has a persistent pattern of losing or misplacing things needed for tasks, which would further support ADHD inattentive type over nonspecific concentration difficulty.
doctor.question: Do you often lose or misplace things you need, like keys, glasses, papers, or tools?

target_item.name: Losing_Items
target_item.manifestation: I spend more time than I should hunting for my keys, reading glasses, tape measure, or the little bag of card-game supplies, even when I just had them in my hand a few minutes before.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about often losing or misplacing needed items such as keys, glasses, papers, or tools, which matches this symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do, more than I’d like to admit. It’s not usually something huge, but it’s those everyday things I need right then — my keys, my reading glasses, a tape measure if I’m doing something around the house, or that little bag I keep with card-game supplies in it.

What gets me is sometimes I’ll swear I just had the thing in my hand. Like I’ll set my glasses down for just a minute, and then a few minutes later I’m walking around checking the table, the counter, my pockets, the chair beside me — and it turns out they’re somewhere obvious, but not where I thought. Same with keys. I don’t lose them for days or anything, but I spend more time than I should hunting around for them.

It’s a little irritating because it’s usually when I’m trying to get ready to leave or get started on something, and then I’m delayed because I have to stop and do this whole search routine.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient shows a hallmark ADHD symptom of failing to follow through on instructions due to distractibility rather than a nonspecific concentration complaint.
doctor.question: Do you often have trouble finishing tasks after someone gives you instructions, even when you understand what to do?

target_item.reason: The question is most directly about difficulty following through on instructions and finishing tasks, which is not one of the listed symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d say that happens a lot, at least not in a clear-cut way. If someone gives me instructions and I understand them, I can usually do the thing, especially if it’s fairly straightforward.

Where it gets a little fuzzy is if the instructions have a lot of parts, or if there’s a delay between being told and actually doing it. Then I might need to think back through it, like, “Wait, what was the order again?” But I don’t know if that’s really trouble finishing so much as needing a minute to get myself lined up.

If someone says, “Do this, then this, then this,” I generally get what they mean. I don’t usually just stop because I didn’t follow through. I guess I haven’t noticed that as one of my bigger issues, if that makes sense.
